extracted.intended_audience: scholars, social scientists, and policy-makers interested in peer review, grant evaluation, and the sociology of academic assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Inductive, sociological analysis of the criteria and practices by which grant proposals and academic work are evaluated across disciplines, emphasizing how meanings of criteria (e.g., significance, fairness) are constructed in practice. Useful for researchers studying peer review or practitioners wanting to understand disciplinary variation in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of the project
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the project is judged to be 'significant' — past research found that significance strongly influences funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author probes what reviewers and panel members from different disciplines mean by 'significance,' emphasizing that its meaning varies by discipline and is subject to interpretation rather than a stable metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic virtuosity and display of cultural capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The stylistic quality of the work and demonstration of cultural capital are treated as criteria of evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria capture non-cognitive aspects (form, rhetorical skill, markers of taste/status) that evaluators may use alongside or instead of strictly methodological or empirical criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the work is empirically robust and evidence-based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical soundness is cited alongside methodological sophistication as a core evaluative dimension, but its interpretation can vary across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological sophistication
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the rigor, appropriateness, and sophistication of methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological quality is a central criterion but is read differently in different disciplines; the book analyzes how meanings of methodology are produced in evaluation settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universalistic norms / consensus in science
rubrics_metrics.description: Mertonian ideal that evaluation should be based on universalistic, impersonal criteria and scientific consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The literature often frames evaluation as achievable by removing particularistic considerations; the author interrogates this by showing evaluation uses multiple competing criteria and is not purely universalistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularistic characteristics (age, reputation, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments based on author characteristics such as age and reputation that may influence evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies ask whether such 'irrelevant' characteristics affect evaluation. The author notes these particularistic considerations are a focus of prior research but argues evaluation cannot be reduced to simply removing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Halo effects and Matthew effects (prestige and reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The way in which reputation and association confer additional prestige or advantage in evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halo and Matthew effects describe how reputation can skew assessments; the book situates these effects among multiple coexisting evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived fairness and enactment of fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Not just fairness as an abstract ideal, but what is perceived as fair and the actions panelists take to enact and sustain fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author examines how panelists promote and perform fairness in deliberation, showing fairness itself is constructed and sustained through interactional practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparables and path dependency in judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluators compare proposals using shifting 'comparables,' and early frames/priming shape subsequent judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Path dependency explains how initial comparisons and 'priming' influence later evaluations (analogy to real-estate comparables); criteria for comparison change as proposals are regrouped and re-compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion work, self-concept, and face-saving
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional labor by evaluators (pleasure, saving face, maintaining self-concept) is intrinsic to the evaluation process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to views that emotions corrupt evaluation, the author argues extra-cognitive elements are necessary for evaluation to proceed smoothly and are integral to how academics enact standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homophilic judgments (preference for similar work/people)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency for evaluators to favor work or authors similar to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author finds homophilic judgments are pervasive across social sciences and humanities and influence evaluative practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary differences in evaluative practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Different disciplines use different standards, styles of justification, and modes of assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fields with low functional dependence and high strategic dependence (e.g., English literature) judge contributions in diffuse, tacit ways relying on personal contacts; the book analyzes these cross-disciplinary contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependency and task uncertainty shaping evaluation (Whitley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Field-level properties such as dependence (need to pool resources) and task uncertainty predict how evaluation and power relations are organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater need to pool resources leads to competition over reputation and more reliance on diffuse, tacit judgments; evaluative styles follow organizational and epistemic characteristics of fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise, credibility, and closure of controversies (science studies concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of claims of expertise, credibility of actors, and the processes that stabilize facts or close controversies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insights from Latour, Woolgar, and Collins inform how evaluators establish credibility and settle disputes, affecting what is counted as quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on personal contacts and tacit knowledge in diffuse fields
rubrics_metrics.description: In some fields evaluators rely heavily on personal networks and tacit knowledge as evaluative resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is particularly noted for disciplines characterized by diffuse, tacit judgment styles, where explicit codified criteria are less central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pluralism of standards and communication styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation draws on a combination of standards and styles of argument; no single predefined logic of justification suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following new French pragmatism, the author emphasizes coordinated action and plural ways panelists make arguments while promoting particular conceptions of fairness; an inductive approach is recommended rather than imposing pre-defined logics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisficing / organizational constraints leading to 'good enough' decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-making is often satisficing rather than optimal, due to organizational constraints and the need for timely allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author highlights how institutional pressures produce 'good enough' choices and shape evaluative practices and standards in panels.
